1:
Three explain why the narrative stands here. John Gill says it is inserted from Kings and Chronicles to illustrate and confirm the prophecies before it. Adam Clarke says the same at more length: it affords the best light to many of them and is almost necessary to introduce the next chapter, God’s answer to a prayer unintelligible without it; these chapters are a different copy of the same narration, the differences largely copyists’ mistakes, so that the two correct each other. John Calvin makes it a seal. The prophet had threatened the calamity and promised the deliverance; both were accomplished, and the record was kept so that he might afterwards be the more believed. Calvin then presses the timing: Hezekiah had just purged the temple and called the people back to the true worship, and precisely then the land is invaded and he is shut up in his city as in a prison. Judged by the flesh God seems unjust; but the king was not punished for carelessness or luxury, much less superstition—his faith was being tried.

The date is contested. Charles Ellicott reports that nearly all who read the Assyrian inscriptions rectify it: they fix the campaign in the third year of the invader, coinciding not with the fourteenth but with the twenty-seventh year of the king of Judah, the received figure arising from an editor who assumed the illness followed the ruin of the army and reckoned the added fifteen years back from the death. Keil and Delitzsch take up a related suggestion, that the revolt came at the accession because the king held his kingdom in fief from his God, so obedience to a temporal monarch would in his case be sin; they reject it as out of accord with the prophet’s own view. Calvin notices a disturbance nearer the surface: all the cities are said to be taken, yet the envoy is sent from a city still besieged; he answers that historical connection is frequently disturbed, and a part often put for the whole.

Ellicott takes the envoy’s name for a title, probably chief officer or cup-bearer, like the other two, and sets the scene: Hezekiah had already sued for peace and paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, emptying his treasury and the temple’s and stripping the gold from the doors—and peace was not to be had at that price. Calvin says the same of the second demand: such gulfs are insatiable, and the harder terms were meant partly to torment the king, partly to furnish occasion for war. Gill notes the perfidy plainly: the money was taken to withdraw the army, and the army then sent to the capital. Ellicott adds that the place chosen, where the prophet had stood before another king thirty years before, commanded one end of the aqueduct, so the water supply could be threatened.

Two read the delegation. Ellicott finds it significant that the man now over the house had lately displaced its former holder, now reduced to scribe, and traces it to the prophet’s influence; Calvin sees that promotion apparently failing, since the man God raised is sent out as a suppliant to surrender, and notes that good men were so scarce the king had to send with him the officer he knew to be treacherous. Matthew Henry declines the history and takes the lessons. A people may be in the way of their duty and still meet distress; a reformation done by halves invites the affliction that quickens it. We must never think our mountain stands so strong it cannot be moved: a king pious and prudent, who had lately bought his peace, had an army poured into his country all of a sudden. And the enemies of God’s people work by frightening them out of their confidence in him, and are always ready to claim a commission from him for what they do.
4:
John Calvin sets the tone of the interview: the three ambassadors, attended by what magnificence the kingdom still had, were not merely repulsed but treated with disdain and loaded with reproaches, as though the king stood convicted of wicked revolt. Some take the particle in the summons for a word of entreaty; Calvin objects that entreaty would be unsuitable in so proud a man, who speaks in the ordinary language of those who lay conditions on the vanquished. The envoy speaks in his master’s name and extols his greatness to the skies, calling him the great king because by his power he eclipsed all others; and by such thunderbolts of words the besieged king might well have been overthrown, shut up as he was in the city.

The taunt about words divides the readings. John Gill takes the phrase for a word of the lips, the fruit of the lips not the heart, and reports two ways of filling it out: prayer to God, which he assigns to Kimchi, or the eloquence with which the king encouraged his soldiers. Adam Clarke notes that fourteen manuscripts and the parallel copy put the verb in the second person, and paraphrases the sneer: thou talkest of counsels, but hast none; of strength, but there is none with thee. Calvin canvasses the expositions and rejects the one that makes the words prayers as far-fetched and unnatural. He takes it instead of a beautiful and elegant style used to keep the people to their duty, of no use for war, where wisdom and courage are needed; it might, he allows, glance at the Egyptians, liberal in promising mountains of gold and giving nothing, but he reserves that for the next verse.

On the broken reed Gill points to the cane on the banks of the Nile, and Clarke calls it a weakened, faithless ally that will take subsidy after subsidy and do nothing for it. Calvin lays out the three steps of the figure: a staff of reed for weakness, a broken staff by way of amplification, and a staff that so far from supporting pierces the hand. He insists the charge is a slander, since the pious king had not in fact leaned there. What he grants is that God justly allowed a rebellious people to hear this from such a mouth: the prophet had condemned the Egyptian alliance in severe terms and they refused the reproof, so they deserved the enemy for their instructor. Calvin then marks the difference between the two kinds of rebuke. When God dissuades us from confidence in the flesh he brings us low and at once holds out a remedy; when the adversary blames a vain hope he drives to despair and substitutes another as bad, striking down the hope in Egypt only to set the king of Assyria in its place.

The last stroke turns the reformation into evidence. Charles Ellicott explains it from the invader’s religion: on that standard a god was honoured in proportion as his sanctuaries were multiplied, and the envoy had found everywhere high places where the God of Judah had been worshipped and which Hezekiah had desecrated—so how could such a man hope for that God’s protection. Clarke notes two ancient manuscripts and three versions with the plural, if ye say, and renders the last clause as a restriction, to worship only before this altar. Calvin reduces the whole speech to a three-part argument: the king cannot trust himself, cannot trust Egypt, and has forfeited God, so that every assistance divine and human is taken from him at a stroke. He adds that the slander was aimed past the king at the fickle multitude, many of whom still leaned to the old superstition and could be told their troubles came of setting aside ancient ceremonies—an accusation, he remarks, still made in his own day against those who abolished traditions long in use.
8:
The offer of horses is read as a jeer by all who touch it. Charles Ellicott would render the opening not as give pledges but as make a wager, and thinks the sentence a taunt interpolated in the middle of the official message: there was something absurd in the notion of Judah coming out strong in cavalry, and the question is whether they had two thousand men who could manage horses supposing they were given them. John Gill keeps the pledges and lists the possibilities—hostages for future fidelity, or a mingling that means coming to terms, or a mingling that means joining battle. John Calvin reads the whole as irony and would put the verb in the subjunctive: were I to give thee two thousand horses, thou wouldst not find riders for them. The horses are not offered out of respect or kindness but to shake the heart further, and the conclusion pressed on the king is that nothing remains but to lay aside the war and promise constant obedience.

The taunt about the least captain works the same arithmetic. Gill explains that the smallest officer had, on Kimchi’s account, two thousand men under him, so that a king who could not mount two thousand riders was no match for the least of them, still less for the army. He rejects the suggestion that the envoy means himself: the invading king would not have sent an inferior officer as principal speaker, and the self-deprecation would not suit so imperious a man. Calvin adds the tactical point—the boast is made because the great king was still detained at the siege of Lachish, and the Jews were not to take courage from his absence when his lieutenants alone were claimed to be enough.

The claim of a divine commission is where the readings part. Gill takes it as insinuation meant to intimidate, and concedes just enough: the invader had not come up without God’s knowledge, nor without his will to chastise, but he had no commission to destroy, as the event showed. Adam Clarke guesses at a source, that some apostate priest may have told him the God of Judah had given him the charge. Ellicott offers three possibilities—an empty boast, or the prophet’s own teaching that God had brought this king in as an instrument having become known, or a dream that the God of Judah was angry at the destruction of the high places—and observes that the man assumes the character of a defender of the faith, as his own inscriptions do, which are conspicuous for claiming divine sanction for his wars.

Calvin turns the boast into the chapter’s hardest lesson. The argument is that the king contends not with a mortal but with God, so that resistance is fighting against God and every effort is fruitless; and the answer is not that piety is always rewarded here. The Lord does not recompense godliness with earthly rewards, and it would be an unsuitable recompense if he did, since on that reckoning our condition would not differ from the reprobate’s. Calvin sees the adversary speaking through the mouth before them, transformed into an angel of light: the Spirit himself says that the strength of man is frail and that whoever leans on it seeks his own destruction, and the envoy says the same thing, discoursing as though he held the prophetic office. We must therefore distinguish wisely when God speaks and when his name is falsely assumed. The slander is the sharpest part of the trial, since we want our integrity known and take it ill when others read our conduct otherwise; but an upright conscience ought to be to us like a brazen wall.
11:
The request to change languages is the hinge. John Gill notes the singular verb: one of the three spoke for the rest, probably the man over the house. Charles Ellicott supplies the diplomacy and the misgiving. The officers knew the little faith of their people, and had perhaps fears of their own: might the townsmen on the wall hear an echo of the prophet’s words, and lose heart, feeling they fought against the God chastising them? The Aramaic was common ground for both embassies as the language of trade; the envoy seems to have had three tongues, the ministers two, the men on the wall one. He leaves it open whether the Jews’ language means simply Hebrew, which the prophet elsewhere calls the language of Canaan, or a dialect of Judah, noting that dialects spring up quickly and the narrower sense occurs elsewhere only after the exile. John Calvin compares that older form to the French of his own day, current at courts across a wide region.

Calvin measures the humiliation. That a king should entreat so humbly the servant of his enemy shows how far he was depressed, and the refusal was the more shameful because what was asked was of little value; forgetful almost of his rank he tries every modesty, and the rage went unappeased through no fault of his. Calvin draws the rule: under unjust violence let us not be ashamed to yield our rights and supplicate humbly. The submission is what makes the sequel remarkable: a rescue from ordinary danger would be far less so. Matthew Henry takes two lessons from the request. While princes and counsellors have public matters under debate it is not fair to appeal to the people, reasons of state being secret things of which the vulgar are incompetent judges; to incense subjects against their rulers by base insinuation is not doing as one would be done by. And proud scorners, the fairer they are spoken to, commonly speak the fouler: nothing could have been said more mildly, and rough answers to soft ones render evil for good.

The reply is the coarsest thing here. Keil and Delitzsch supply the point: the rulers were exposing their people to a siege that would bring the most dreadful famine. Ellicott says the brutality has hardly a parallel in history short of a statesman of his own century telling a besieged city to stew in its own gravy; he reads it as a claim that the besiegers could cut off food and water alike. Adam Clarke works on the words: one old version reads a negative, that they may not eat, which he thinks perhaps right, while many manuscripts substitute the water, his own adding a modest marginal circumlocution. Calvin reads the tone: he speaks like a conqueror and addresses the king as a slave, which shows he was sent not to offer terms but to force an unconditional surrender.

He then turned from the ministers to the wall. Gill sees him raise himself and strain his voice to the utmost, using the very request that betrayed their fear to stir the people to mutiny and force a surrender of the city. Calvin finds the attitude itself insolent, a man placing himself where he could be better seen; but what appals him is the language. That the holy tongue, consecrated to heavenly wisdom, should be prostituted to blasphemy was a sore temptation to weak minds, and teaches that no enemies are more destructive than those who speak our own language—men who learn our way of speaking to insinuate themselves into weak ears, and who within thirty years had gone from a barbarous idiom to cloaking impiety in the ordinary words of Scripture. It is the adversary’s habit, he adds, to magnify the power of enemies and make dangers look larger than they are; the remedy is to set God’s power against them.
14:
John Calvin notices the grammar of the insult: the speaker keeps the great title for his own master and names the king of Judah without any title, as a private person. He calls it imposture and deception that this king should rely on God’s favour and urge his subjects to the same confidence—venom vomited at God, Calvin says, as much as slander of the man; and the same charge was made in his own century against those who taught people to hope in the true God, coming as it does from the same inventor of slander. He grants what is true in it—that they could not be delivered by the king’s hand unless God assisted—but the king never claimed otherwise, and the enemy needed some pretext, as slanderers do, of the plausible kind that deceives when not closely examined. John Gill notes that the envoy speaks as the king himself, whose general he was, to command the greater awe.

The second stroke is aimed at the trust itself. Gill says the king had trusted God and laboured by example and argument to bring his people to do the same, and that the envoy, sensible of it, feared this more than anything else and pressed the point above all others. Calvin sees the technique: the man does not openly deny that God can help if he chooses, but by sapping the foundation of their faith reduces that power to nothing, so the people may submit as if in despair. Adam Clarke adds that a body of manuscripts supplies a conjunction at the head of the last clause.

Then comes the bribe, and Calvin gives it his closest analysis. The offer flatters with the allurements of a more comfortable life, and nothing makes us readier to revolt from God than the appearance of advantage. The argument is that a hope which cannot be seen should be exchanged for a good in hand—men are so impatient of delay that they prefer an immediate advantage to a distant one—and Calvin calls this the daily sophistry, since we hope for what we do not see, and the taunt why dost thou hope in vain is the adversary’s own. Behind the named king, he says, the comparison is between God and the invader, one showing his good things at a distance, the other presenting them now. Clarke reads the word for agreement as a blessing, meaning a ransom for the city and the yearly tribute already promised; Calvin takes it figuratively for a present and notes an old version rendering it simply as making peace, adding that the friendly word cloaks a bondage hateful in itself, since to revolt from a pious king whom God had appointed could not happen without denying God.

The last condition is the harshest. Calvin points out that peace is now to be had only by banishment, which meant abandoning the worship of God and quitting the inheritance he had given; and because the word was harsh the speaker covers it by promising a country as fertile as their own, drawing a veil over their eyes so they should think they lost nothing. What he cunningly passes over is everything worth having—the worship of God, the temple, the kingdom, the order of holy government—and without these, Calvin asks, what happiness can there be, when to dwell in the house of God is better than all the luxuries of the world. Gill reports the guesses at the land intended, one naming a region thought to resemble Judea in situation and fruitfulness, another naming Africa, and answers that none was named because none could be named like Canaan; the removal was the usual policy of conquerors, so the conquered should have no expectation of recovering their own country. Clarke notes that the parallel copy adds a clause here: a land of oil-olive and of honey, that ye may live and not die.
18:
The taunt widens into blasphemy, and John Calvin marks the change of ground. The speaker had claimed to come as God’s own servant; now he insults God openly, as wicked men do, concealing their scorn at first until the Lord constrains them to discover the venom of their heart. Having beaten the nations that relied on their gods, he supposes he has beaten the gods, and so puts his own strength into conflict with the power of the living God. Calvin will not let him off as a man merely exposing the weakness of idols: he does not ridicule the superstition of the nations but pours contempt, in the idols, on the power of God—as a tyrant of old who mocked his own gods was defying God, attacking against his conscience such a deity as his mind could hold. The deeper blasphemy is the levelling: to make the immortal Creator one of a multitude is to confound truth with falsehood, glory with shame, heaven with earth. Charles Ellicott says as much without the heat: the man speaks the natural language of polytheism, in which the God of Israel was a simple national deity among gods many, while the gods of Assyria stood supreme.

John Gill notes how carefully the title of king is withheld, so Hezekiah appears not as their lawful sovereign but as a deceiver to be guarded against. On the cities named, Gill places them in Syria, one of them thought to be the place afterwards called Antiochia and Epiphania, the other perhaps founded by a people named in the old table of nations. Calvin makes the choice tactical: they are the neighbouring cities, whose fall was better known and bit deeper—look at these two kingdoms subdued, which had their own gods for guardians, and will your God resist me?

Ellicott supplies the answer the question was designed to get. To modern ears the where invites only an echo; but on the invaders’ own practice the answer was that those gods were to be seen in the temples of Assyria, as trophies of its victories. He places the last of the cities on the left bank of the Euphrates, probably the sun-city in which the Noah of an old mythology was said to have hidden the sacred books before the flood. Adam Clarke keeps to the apparatus: many manuscripts add a conjunction, the parallel copy adds two further names, and the copulative in the last clause is unexpressed in three ancient versions, which he thinks favour a conjecture reading it as an interrogative particle instead.

Calvin ends with the logic of the boast. He would not make the last clause a question at all but read it ironically—yes, as the gods of the nations delivered their worshippers, so will your God assist you. The insolence comes of not seeing that adversity is God punishing sin; the conqueror argues that because he beat a nation he is the stronger, never seeing that he was appointed executioner of an anger not his own, then climbs higher, reasoning that because he beat those over whom God presided he has beaten God. This, Calvin says, is the very thing foretold when the invader was called the rod of God’s indignation, who thought not so. The lesson is to look past the instrument: if the wicked prove stronger, the arm of God is not broken, we simply do not deserve his help. And he notes the last irony. This man kept some form of piety, being afterwards killed in the temple of his god while worshipping there; but one who treads the Creator underfoot along with the gods of the nations would not have scrupled, at the right moment, to do the same to his own idol. Gill puts the point in a line: not one of them, it is suggested, ever delivered anything.
21:
The silence is read four ways. John Gill insists it was not the silence of men confounded: they could have proved that the Lord was greater than the gods of the nations, and could have thrown the broken faith of the treaty back in his face, but they waived it all; no doubt they said something to him, since otherwise what were they sent as commissioners for, but to the blasphemies and the menaces they made no answer. Charles Ellicott attributes the silence to an order: the king seems to have commanded it, distrusting either the wisdom of his ambassadors or the effect any chance word might have on the garrison and the people, since the only words they had so far spoken had made matters infinitely worse. Adam Clarke notes that the subject of the verb is uncertain, and that the people is supplied from the parallel copy on the authority of one manuscript.

John Calvin sets the scene first: the king, with hardly any strength or means of defence left, is struck dumb while an enemy insults him, and the ambassadors sent to soothe that enemy, having failed, are enjoined to be silent lest they provoke a savage beast already too much excited. On the ambiguity Clarke noticed he decides for the men on the wall, who were sharply piqued by the taunts and yet were not provoked to quarrel, because they obeyed the king’s command—which he thinks a peculiar kindness of God, that they should be so disposed to obedience when matters were desperate. But he raises the obvious objection against himself. We ought not to conceal our sentiments when wicked men mock and reproach God, even at the risk of our lives; we owe him at least the testimony that we cannot patiently endure his honour attacked. His answer is that this silence was not consent. The reproaches gave them deep pain, and it would have been of no avail to debate with such a man, so the people reckoned it enough to meet his impertinence with silent groans. Calvin makes two rules of it: amidst bitter strife and confused noise the truth will not be heard, so we are not always to contend; and yet our silence has no excuse unless we somehow declare that the dishonouring of God’s name is what distresses us most. It is no despicable courage, he adds, when we cannot utter a syllable, still not to flinch but to remain quietly in our place.

The torn clothes are that declaration. Ellicott calls the act the natural expression of their horror at the blasphemy: they would not answer it, and trusted instead to the effect of a silent protest on the minds of the people who had heard it. Calvin agrees that the gesture proves they were neither approving nor conniving through fear, though he makes one exception, of the officer he judges destitute of piety, who put on the dress of mourning with the others out of shame and as a matter of form. He notes that the custom belonged to nations of a warmer temperament than his own, which show more vehemence in gesture, bearing and dress than the inhabitants of cold countries. And he draws a test from it: these men had taken no notice of the insults offered to themselves and tore their garments only when God was reproached, whereas whoever is quick to resent a private affront and unmoved at the dishonouring of God’s name shows that he has no zeal or piety at all. Gill simply names the first of the commissioners going back to the king.
